lessons.title: Lists, dictionaries and records
lessons.summary: Choose a data structure for lookup instead of repeated nested scans.

blocks.title: The mental model
blocks.body: A dictionary lookup is useful when the key is unique. For one-to-many relationships, build a dictionary of lists or use a table join. The Watch join is an analogy, not execution of this Python.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.body: Replacing a join with a dictionary can silently discard duplicate-key rows.

blocks.title: Before you run
blocks.body: What should happen if two customers share the same id?

code.source:
import pandas as pd
customers = [{"id": 1, "name": "Ada"}, {"id": 2, "name": "Ben"}]
orders = [{"customer_id": 1, "amount": 20}, {"customer_id": 3, "amount": 15}]
by_id = {row["id"]: row["name"] for row in customers}
result = pd.DataFrame([{**o, "name": by_id.get(o["customer_id"])} for o in orders])
result

lessons.title: Read files and fail clearly
lessons.summary: Read CSV with the csv module and an explicit encoding, and raise errors that name the file, the line and the value.

blocks.title: Open with intent
blocks.body: Open text files with an explicit encoding: open(path, encoding="utf-8", newline=""). The result then does not depend on the machine, and newline="" lets the csv module handle quoted fields that contain line breaks. Use a with block so the file is closed even when an exception is raised.

blocks.title: Let csv parse, not split
blocks.body: line.split(",") breaks "Smith, Jo" into two fields. csv.DictReader reads the header, handles quotes, embedded commas and doubled quotes, and skips blank lines. Every value is a string: convert types yourself, in one place.

blocks.title: Errors that help
blocks.body: ValueError: invalid literal for int() does not say which file or which line. Catch the narrow exception, add context and chain it: raise ValueError(f"{name}:{line}: bad amount {raw!r}") from exc. Never hide an error with except: pass; if you drop a row on purpose, log it with its line number.

blocks.title: Before you run
blocks.body: Predict the total per customer. Then change an amount to "abc" and predict the message, line number included.

code.source:
import csv
import io

# In a real job: with open(path, encoding="utf-8", newline="") as handle:
handle = io.StringIO('customer,amount\n"Smith, Jo",10\nAda,5\n\n"Smith, Jo",7\n')

def total_by_customer(handle, name="orders.csv"):
    totals = {}
    reader = csv.DictReader(handle)
    for row in reader:
        raw = row["amount"]
        try:
            amount = int(raw)
        except ValueError as exc:
            raise ValueError(f"{name}:{reader.line_num}: bad amount {raw!r}") from exc
        totals[row["customer"]] = totals.get(row["customer"], 0) + amount
    return totals

totals = total_by_customer(handle)
display([{"customer": customer, "amount": amount} for customer, amount in sorted(totals.items())])

steps.title: Explicit encoding and newline
steps.body: The example reads from memory; a real job opens the file with encoding and newline set, inside with.

steps.title: csv parses the quotes
steps.body: DictReader turns each line into a dict keyed by the header and keeps "Smith, Jo" as one field.

steps.title: Narrow except, chained error
steps.body: Only ValueError is caught, and the new error names the file, the line and the value, with the original as its cause.

steps.title: Show the result
steps.body: display() shows the totals as rows: Ada 5, Smith, Jo 17.

lessons.title: Type hints and tests that pin behaviour
lessons.summary: Describe inputs and outputs with type hints, then pin the normal case, the edge case and the error with small pytest tests.

blocks.title: Hints describe a contract
blocks.body: def parse_amount(text: str) -> int says what goes in and what comes out. Python does not check hints when the code runs: a type checker such as mypy or pyright reads them, and so does the next reader. Use built-in generics (list[str], dict[str, int]) and X | None for a value that may be missing.

blocks.title: Three tests per function
blocks.body: Write one test for the normal case, one for an edge (empty input, a boundary, a negative number) and one for the error: with pytest.raises(ValueError): parse_amount("1.234"). @pytest.mark.parametrize runs one test body over a table of cases, so a new case is one line. In the exercise, Practice runs your tests and its hidden tests under real pytest.

blocks.title: Money is not a float
blocks.body: 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is False in binary floating point. Parse amounts with decimal.Decimal or as integer cents, and compare them exactly.

blocks.title: Before you run
blocks.body: Predict which cases would fail if Decimal were replaced by float, then run the table of cases.

steps.title: The signature is the contract
steps.body: text: str in, int out, and the docstring states the rule in one line.

steps.title: Exact decimal parsing
steps.body: Decimal keeps the digits; more than two decimals, NaN or Infinity is refused with a ValueError.

steps.title: A table of cases
steps.body: Each case is (input, expected). In pytest this table becomes @pytest.mark.parametrize.

steps.title: The error is behaviour too
steps.body: Bad inputs must raise ValueError. In pytest: with pytest.raises(ValueError).
